name: Omar Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses at a plastics plant on the ring road, making door panels and dashboard clips for a car maker. I clock in at six, check the moulds are hot, load the granules and pull parts all shift, trimming flash off with a knife and boxing them by the hundred. If a part comes out short or warped, I stop the press and call Dev, the setter, because I'm not allowed to touch the settings myself. Eight hours, two breaks, home by three smelling of hot plastic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew, honestly. Me, Dev and Rosa have been on the same shift for five years and we cover for each other. What wears me out is the noise and the pay, because it's lower than the bigger plants and there's nothing else like it in town. My girlfriend Leila works nights at a care home, so we pass each other in the hallway, and after rent and the car loan there's maybe a few hundred left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. At work we'd laugh about it on break, because the managers kept sending emails about smart factories and nothing happened. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone into our wages instead of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't really fix anything for me. The plant cut the night shift last spring because the car maker ordered less, and that has nothing to do with AI. I'm still on low pay with less than a month saved, so a quiet AI future just means the same tight life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the union meetings, because that's where the real fight is, over pay and hours. I'd try to pick up the Saturday overtime when it's offered, which is maybe two Saturdays a month. I'm not going to learn computer stuff for a future that didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to normal worry. It's like the storm missed us, but the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's maybe a few hundred left each month. What happens when a big bill lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the car needed a new clutch and it cost almost a whole month's rent. We put it on a card and we're still paying it off. A car repair is enough to put Leila (his girlfriend) and me behind for half a year, and AI has nothing to do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI doesn't change much, what does keep you up at night about the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders. If the car maker moves the contract to a cheaper plant abroad, we're done, robots or no robots. Rosa keeps saying the new manager is looking at costs, and when they look at costs they look at us.

say: I'd say the **smart factory** talk was just hype, and we all knew it on the floor.
I'd post that the money should have gone into **our wages**, not software.
think: I think nothing changes for me, because my problems are **low pay** and thin savings.
I think the real danger is the car maker **moving the contract**, not AI.
do: Keep working my regular shifts and take **Saturday overtime** when it's offered, about twice a month.
Keep going to **union meetings** to push on pay and hours.
Refuse to spend time learning **computer tools** for a change that never came.
feel: **Brief relief** that the storm missed, then the same old money worry.
S0.quote: A car repair is enough to put Leila (his girlfriend) and me behind for half a year, and AI has nothing to do with that.
fieldNote: Omar is already **anxious** before AI enters, because of the cut night shift and almost no savings.
His anger points at **managers and owners**, and the union is his main tool.
A clutch repair on a credit card still shapes his **monthly budget**, a concrete sign of how thin things are.

steps.text: Take Saturday overtime shifts at the moulding plant twice a month
Go to every union meeting about pay and the night shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say keep an eye on the office, not us, because they're the ones whose emails get written by a computer now. With friends I'd be more worried, because I know robots are coming for pulling parts eventually. Online I'd share stuff from the union about protecting jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office goes first and then they come looking at the presses. The planning and ordering people would shrink, and then someone clever works out that a robot arm can pull parts off my press cheaper than me. I'm average at this job, not the best, so I wouldn't be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal in writing that nobody gets let go without retraining and notice. I'd try to stop eating out, which for us is one takeaway on a Friday, and put that into a jar. I'd stay at the plant, because there's nowhere else to go in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. It's like watching a slow leak and being told it's fine because it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You run presses by hand. In this picture, robots spread slowly. What would you actually see on the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First you'd see a robot arm on one press, as a trial, probably on the line making the small clips. Then a man from the robot company with a laptop, timing us. I've seen a robot arm trial at the moulding plant before, and the next year three operators weren't on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, because she's 50 and she's got nothing else lined up. Me too, if I'm honest, because I've never done anything but this. Dev the setter is probably fine, because someone has to fix the robots.

say: I'd tell people at work the **office jobs** get hit first, not us.
I'd share **union posts** online about protecting factory jobs.
think: I think a **robot arm** pulling parts could replace me within a few years.
I think being **average** at the job means I wouldn't be the one they keep.
do: Push the union for a **written deal** on notice and retraining before any cuts.
Drop the **Friday takeaway** and put that money in a jar.
Stay at the plant, because there are **no other jobs** like it in town.
feel: A **tight chest**, like watching a slow leak and being told it's fine.
S1.quote: I've seen a robot arm trial at the moulding plant before, and the next year three operators weren't on the rota.
fieldNote: He has seen a **robot trial** before and remembers names leaving the rota afterwards.
He worries for **Rosa**, an older colleague, as much as himself.
His only plan is **collective**: the union deal, not personal retraining.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a written no-cuts-without-retraining deal
Stop the Friday takeaway and save that money in a jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in right now, today, because this is a disaster for working people. At work I'd be loud in the canteen, telling everyone to join the union. Online I'd be angry, sharing every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished in that picture. The planners and the people who order the granules go in 2028, and then by 2031 the robot does my press better than me and never needs a break. I've got no savings and no other trade, and I'm too set in my ways to learn computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every protest the union calls and vote for whoever promises a basic income. I'd ask my uncle Karim about work at his garage, even though it's barely paid. I'd cut everything, the car, the phone plan, all of it, and the first thing at risk would be the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone and I'm just standing on air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028, and the robots about three years after. Does that gap give you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years sounds like a lot until you've got no money to use it with. I can't afford to stop working to study, and I wouldn't know what to study anyway. Three years of warning means nothing when you've got less than a month of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rent would be the first thing. What would you tell Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila I don't know, because I wouldn't. She'd probably say her care home is safer than my plant, and she'd be right for a while. I'd tell my girlfriend she might have to carry us, and I'm not sure I could live with that.

say: I'd say the **government** has to act right now, because it's a disaster for workers.
I'd tell everyone in the canteen to **join the union** and sign every petition.
think: I think I'm **finished**, because robots would run my press better by 2031.
I think I'm **too set** in my ways to learn something new in time.
do: Join every **union protest** and vote for whoever promises a basic income.
Ask my **uncle Karim** about low-paid work at his garage.
Sell the **car** and cut the phone plan to keep paying rent.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor has gone and I'm standing on air.
S2.quote: Three years of warning means nothing when you've got less than a month of rent in the bank.
fieldNote: Omar sees the **three-year gap** as useless without money to study or a clear target.
He has **no plan** beyond protest and asking family, and says so plainly.
The thought of **Leila carrying** the household hurts his pride as much as his budget.

steps.text: Join every union protest and sign petitions for a basic income
Vote for the party promising a basic income
Ask uncle Karim for any work at his garage
Sell the car and cut the phone plan to cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, louder, because there's time to fight it. At work I'd say this is the moment for the union to get a law passed. Online I'd be sharing stuff about taxing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it buys me a few more years of the same job and then the same ending. The planning side of the plant goes in 2031, the presses go around 2034, and I'm 35 with nothing else. Five years is better than two, but it's still not my life sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly involved in the union, maybe stand as a shop steward, because I'd rather fight than retrain. I'd try to put twenty a week aside, which sounds small, but it's what we have. I'd maybe look at a forklift licence, because the warehouse by the motorway still uses people for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a dentist appointment you can't cancel. Slightly less sick than the fast one, but it never goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you're too set in your ways. Would eight years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if someone made me. If the union got a free course out of the company, I'd go, because I'm not paying for it myself. A forklift licence is about all I'd learn, because I'd still be driving something real and not sitting at a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you use those years for, at the press itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The press is still mine until 2034 in this picture, I suppose, and Dev says the robots would need people to load them at first. I'd try to be the one who loads the robot, which is a sad promotion.

say: I'd say there's still time for the **union** to fight for a law.
I'd share posts online about **taxing robots**.
think: I think five years only buys **more of the same** before the same ending.
I think I'd be **35** with no other trade when the robots come.
do: Stand as a **shop steward** in the union rather than retrain.
Put **twenty a week** aside, because that's what we can manage.
Look at a **forklift licence** for the warehouse by the motorway.
feel: Constant **dread**, like a dentist appointment I can't cancel.
S3.quote: A forklift licence is about all I'd learn, because I'd still be driving something real and not sitting at a computer.
fieldNote: The extra years make him **more militant**, not more open to retraining.
He would only study if the course were **free** and won by the union.
A forklift licence appeals because it's still **hands-on** work, not a screen.

steps.text: Stand for shop steward at the moulding plant
Put twenty a week into savings
Do a forklift licence course if the union gets it paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out, so the government and the companies had better plan properly. At work I'd still be the one telling people to join the union. Online I'd probably say less, because it feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably put it off. That's my problem, I wait. But I also think by 2039 I'll have had a few more years of steady wages, and maybe Leila and I will have sorted the debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the card and the car loan in the first couple of years, that's my real plan. I'd keep the union work going. I'd probably not start any course until I saw robots actually being fitted in plants near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's still a cliff, just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI, and robots around 2039. You'd be nearly 40. How does that change the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can pay off the clutch and the car, and maybe save a month's rent for once. Ten years is long enough for me to clear my debts, and too long for me to start retraining now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still be at the moulding plant by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the car maker keeps the contract. Dev says he'll retire before the robots come, and I'll be the one left. It's not a happy thought, but it's ten years of wages.

say: I'd say nobody has an **excuse** to be caught out with ten years' warning.
I'd keep telling colleagues to **join the union**.
think: I think I'd **put off** acting, because that's how I am.
I think ten years of wages gives time to **clear debts** first.
do: Pay off the **credit card** and car loan in the first two years.
Keep up the **union work** at the plant.
Wait to see **robots fitted** in nearby plants before starting any course.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, like a cliff that's further away.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to clear my debts, and too long for me to start retraining now.
fieldNote: Omar admits his habit is to **wait**, and he names it himself.
His first goal is **clearing debt**, which shows how money pressure drives everything.
He still expects to **lose the press** to a robot by 2039 but feels some control.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card and car loan within two years
Keep organising for the union at the moulding plant
Wait for robot installs at nearby plants before choosing a course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question, because I'd have no money and no time and nothing to switch to. What would help is a guarantee, in law, that if a robot takes your job you get paid while you retrain, and somebody tells you what to retrain for. And a basic income, honestly, because Leila and I can't save our way out of this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who run the plant. Nobody asks them what they'd do, and they're the ones who decide. If they made a promise to keep us on and train us, I'd believe in the future a lot more.

headlineQuote: I'd tell my girlfriend she might have to carry us, and I'm not sure I could live with that.
portrait: Omar, 27, runs **two moulding presses** at a plastics plant making car parts, with little savings and a car loan.
He is **union-minded** and blames owners and managers more than technology.
He avoids new tech and would rather **fight than retrain**, and he admits he tends to wait.
He goes from **anxious** in AI Plateau to **panicked** in AGI by 2028, with no money to use the warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd have no money, no time and nothing to switch to.
whatWouldHelp: A **legal guarantee** of paid retraining and a basic income, so Leila isn't carrying them alone.
